title: Longest Evenly Spaced Subsequence
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Pick some of its elements, keeping their original order but skipping any you like. The picked values are evenly spaced if every step from one picked value to the next is the same number d. The step may be zero or negative.

Return the length of the longest evenly spaced subsequence. Any two elements form one, so the answer is at least 2.

examples.why: Skip the 9: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 steps by 3 each time.
Sorting would give 1…6, but the order is fixed. The best you can keep is 6, 4, 2 or 1, 3, 5.
1, 2, 3, 4 with step 1. The picked elements do not have to be next to each other.

hints: A subsequence ending at index i with step d can only be extended by a later element equal to nums[i] + d. What two things describe such a subsequence?
Let len[i][d] be the longest evenly spaced subsequence that ends at index i with step d. How does it relate to some earlier j?
For every pair j < i, set d = nums[i] − nums[j] and len[i][d] = len[j][d] + 1 (or 2 if j has nothing for d). Store one map per index, or an array offset by the smallest possible step.

explain.intuition:
An evenly spaced subsequence is pinned down by where it ends and what its step is. If one ends at index j with step d, and a later element nums[i] equals nums[j] + d, you can append it and get one longer, ending at i with the same step.

So keep, for each index, a table from step to the best length ending there. Looking at every pair j < i fills those tables in O(n²). Each pair says: the step from j to i is d, so whatever chain with step d ended at j can now continue to i. The steps are bounded by the value range (−500 to 500), so an array of 1001 slots per index works as well as a hash map.
steps: Create, for each index i, an empty table len[i] from step to length.
For each i and each j < i: let d = nums[i] − nums[j].
Set len[i][d] = (len[j][d] ?? 1) + 1. A missing entry means the chain is just nums[j], length 1.
Track the largest value written. Return it.
pitfalls: Sorting the array first. Order matters: [6, 4, 2, 1, 3, 5] has answer 3, not 6.
Only extending from adjacent elements. The picked elements can have gaps, so you must consider every earlier j.
Indexing an array by the raw step. Steps can be negative (down to −500), so shift them by an offset or use a hash map.

complexity.space: O(n · range) or O(n²) with maps

solutions.title: Try every starting pair
solutions.idea: Any two elements fix the step. From the second one, greedily take the next element that matches the step; taking the earliest match is never worse.

solutions.title: DP over (end index, step)
solutions.idea: len[i][d] is the longest chain ending at i with step d. Every pair j < i extends len[j][d] by one.

followups: Return the subsequence itself, not just its length.
The step d is given in advance. Can you solve it in O(n) with one hash map?
